notes: Ruling slot 22 = Central African Armed Forces (Bokassa's military regime since the Saint-Sylvestre coup); coalition slot 13 = MESAN, the single party Bokassa kept as his civilian instrument. Goumba's MEDAC in 18. House of Bokassa kept in 23 per MD (clan/dynastic ambitions, no imperial title yet). MD sprites used only for FACA and House of Bokassa.

0.name: Les Fidèles de Dacko
0.text:
Les Fidèles de Dacko are the officials, kinsmen and former ministers who remain attached to David Dacko, the country's first president, overthrown by his cousin Jean-Bédel Bokassa in the Saint-Sylvestre coup on the night of 31 December 1965. Dacko has been held in detention ever since, but his civilian network survives inside the administration.

They stand for a return to civilian single-party rule, close cooperation with France and the West, restored confidence for business and an end to the arbitrary violence of the military regime. Their leverage lies in Dacko's legitimacy as Boganda's successor and in contacts with French officials who see him as a possible alternative.

1.name: Archidiocèse de Bangui
1.text:
The Archdiocese of Bangui heads the Catholic Church in the Central African Republic, the country's largest religious body, with missions, schools and clinics reaching from the Lobaye forests to the northern savanna. Built on the work of the Holy Ghost Fathers, it trained Barthélemy Boganda, the first Ubangian priest and father of the nation, and much of the educated elite.

The Church upholds Christian social teaching, the protection of its schools and of family life, and close ties with France and the West. It is wary of the military regime's violence and of Bokassa's erratic decisions but avoids open confrontation. Its leverage lies in its moral authority, its institutions and the loyalty of Catholic villages.

2.name: Les Évolués de Bangui
2.text:
Les Évolués de Bangui are the French-educated civil servants, lawyers, teachers and clerks of the capital, the first generation formed in mission schools and French universities. Many served under Boganda and Dacko and now staff Bokassa's ministries while watching colleagues dismissed, jailed or beaten on presidential whim.

They favour constitutional government, an independent judiciary, freedom of the press, a professional civil service and an open economy tied to France and the European Economic Community. Pro-Western in outlook, they want the army back in its barracks and elections restored. Their leverage lies in their indispensable administrative skills and their networks among French cooperants and diplomats.

3.name: Union Générale des Travailleurs Centrafricains
3.english: General Union of Central African Workers
3.text:
The General Union of Central African Workers is the country's trade-union federation, bringing together civil servants, teachers, transport workers and employees of French trading houses and plantations. Under the military regime it is closely tied to the single party and its leaders must tread carefully, but rank-and-file members resent late salaries and arbitrary dismissals.

Its programme is social democratic: regular payment of wages, collective agreements, social security, Africanization of skilled posts and the right to strike. It looks to French and international labour movements for support. Its leverage lies in the public sector, the river port and the capital's few factories, which together can bring Bangui to a halt.

4.name: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France
4.english: Federation of Black African Students in France
4.native_full: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France
4.text:
The Federation of Black African Students in France, founded in 1950, is the Marxist-leaning association of African students in France. Its Central African section, a few hundred scholarship holders in Paris and provincial universities, has condemned the military takeover, the execution of Alexandre Banza and the arrests of students, and keeps contacts with Soviet-bloc embassies and the African left.

Its members call for a people's democracy: the army back to barracks, nationalization of the diamond trade and the French concession companies, land and education for peasants and alignment with the socialist camp. Their leverage is modest but real, since the regime depends on these graduates to run its ministries.
4.wiki: Federation of Black African Students in France

5.name: Les Élèves du Lycée Boganda
5.text:
Les Élèves du Lycée Boganda are the radical secondary-school pupils and young teachers of Bangui's leading lycée, together with the first students of the newly founded University of Bangui. They read Fanon, Che Guevara and the African left, mock the regime's pomp in their pamphlets and resent a state that cannot pay for grants, books or jobs.

They demand free education, scholarships paid on time, an end to military rule and a revolutionary transformation of society. Hostile to French influence and suspicious of Moscow alike, they want a people's democracy built from below. Their leverage lies in street protest: school strikes can quickly fill the capital with angry youth.

6.name: Les Banzistes
6.text:
Les Banzistes are the officers and officials once close to Lieutenant-Colonel Alexandre Banza, minister of finance and co-author of the 1966 coup, who was arrested in April 1969 for plotting against Bokassa and executed. His followers have been purged from command, but resentment of the president's personal rule survives in the officer corps and among Banza's Gbaya community in the west.

They want a collegial, nationalist military government free of French tutelage, a disciplined state and an end to Bokassa's personal extravagance. Some look to the Eastern bloc and radical African regimes as alternative patrons. Their leverage is limited to conspiracy, but in an army ruled by fear conspiracy is never far away.

7.name: Les Hommes de Ngaragba
7.text:
Les Hommes de Ngaragba are the security officers, gendarmes and jailers of Bokassa's regime, named after Bangui's central prison, where political detainees are held and where the gendarmerie commander Jean Izamo died in custody after the 1966 coup. They answer directly to the president and watch ministers, officers and students alike.

They believe the state survives only through fear: preventive arrests, informers in every ministry, public punishment and the elimination of rivals. Indifferent to ideology, they would serve any patron who guaranteed their power, and they resent French influence when it shields potential rivals. Their leverage lies in surveillance, the prison and the president's trust.

8.name: Les Libanais de Bangui
8.text:
Les Libanais de Bangui are the Lebanese traders of the capital and the diamond towns, many of them Shia from South Lebanon who came up the Ubangi River from the Congo and Brazzaville. They run shops, transport firms and diamond counters and depend on the goodwill of a president who alternately courts and threatens foreign merchants.

Their notables look to Imam Musa al-Sadr, who in 1969 became head of the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut, and favour an educated, socially engaged Shi'ism. Politically they seek security of property, accommodation with the regime and neutrality between the blocs. Their leverage lies in credit, retail trade and the diamond economy.

9.name: Les Fidèles du Jabal Amil
9.text:
Les Fidèles du Jabal Amil are a handful of young Lebanese Shia in Bangui and Berbérati, named after their ancestral hills in South Lebanon, who follow the militant clerics of Najaf, among them the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. They meet in private prayer gatherings and scorn the commercial caution of their elders.

They hold that clerics must guide the community's public life, condemn the Shah of Iran, Israel and Western influence over Muslim lands and want strict observance of Shia law in the diaspora. They have no following outside a few families. Their leverage rests on the money of sympathetic traders and the visits of preachers from Lebanon.

10.name: Les Imams de Ndélé
10.text:
Les Imams de Ndélé are the Muslim clerics and notables of the northeast, centred on Ndélé, former capital of the sultanate of Dar al-Kuti, and of the Muslim trading quarters of Bangui. Their communities of Runga, Arab, Hausa and Fulani traders and herders form a minority in a largely Christian and animist country.

They preach loyalty to the state in exchange for respect for Islamic courts, mosques and Quranic schools, and seek protection for Muslim merchants and herders from harassment by officials and soldiers. They are attached to Tijani Sufism and wary of radical preachers from Sudan and Chad. Their leverage lies in cross-border trade and the cattle economy.

11.name: Les Héritiers de Senoussi
11.text:
Les Héritiers de Senoussi invoke Muhammad al-Senoussi, the slave-raiding sultan of Dar al-Kuti who ruled the northeast from Ndélé until French troops killed him in 1911. In the remote borderlands with Chad and Sudan, a few preachers and families of his former retinue keep alive the memory of an Islamic state, and some have contacts with the rebels across the Chadian border.

They reject the Christian-dominated republic, call for a sharia state uniting the Muslims of the central Sudan and see the Chadian rebellion as the start of a wider holy war. They are hostile to both blocs. Their leverage is tiny but rests on isolation, cross-border kinship and the state's near absence in the northeast.

12.name: Les Étudiants de Khartoum
12.text:
Les Étudiants de Khartoum are young Central African Muslims who have studied in Sudan, Chad or Egypt and returned to the northeast and to Bangui with ideas of Islamic renewal drawn from the Muslim Brotherhood. Few in number, they teach in Quranic schools and preach in the mosques of the Muslim quarters.

They want better education for Muslims, instruction in Arabic, social solidarity through zakat, reform of popular religious practices and fair representation in a state they see as Christian-dominated. They oppose both secularism and Marxism. Their leverage lies among young Muslim traders and in links to Islamic charities and scholars in Sudan and Egypt.

13.name: Mouvement pour l'Évolution Sociale de l'Afrique Noire
13.english: Movement for the Social Evolution of Black Africa
13.native_full: Mouvement pour l'Évolution Sociale de l'Afrique Noire
13.text:
The Movement for the Social Evolution of Black Africa was founded in 1949 by Barthélemy Boganda and led Ubangi-Shari to independence in 1960. Under David Dacko it became the sole legal party in 1962, and after the Saint-Sylvestre coup Jean-Bédel Bokassa kept it as the civilian instrument of his rule, taking its leadership and filling its organs with loyalists.

MESAN preaches national unity under Boganda's motto 'Zo kwe zo' – every human being is a person – and invokes his dream of a United States of Latin Africa, but in practice it mobilizes crowds, collects dues and distributes patronage. Non-aligned in rhetoric and pragmatic in practice, it draws its leverage from local committees and Boganda's name.
13.wiki: Movement for the Social Evolution of Black Africa

14.name: Les Notables de l'Ouham
14.text:
Les Notables de l'Ouham are the village chiefs, Protestant pastors and leading farmers of the Gbaya, Sara-Kaba and Banda savanna of the northwest and centre, where cotton is the main cash crop. They have little voice in Bangui, but they collect taxes, settle disputes and organize the compulsory cotton campaigns.

They want fair cotton prices, roads and schools, respect for chiefly authority and Protestant missions, and protection from soldiers and tax collectors. They are conservative, attached to rural order and indifferent to Cold War alignments. Their leverage lies in the countryside's food and cotton production and in their ability to mobilize or withhold the villages.

15.name: Les Diamantaires de Bangui
15.text:
Les Diamantaires de Bangui are the foreign buying houses and their African and Lebanese middlemen who control the trade in alluvial diamonds from the Haute-Sangha and Haute-Kotto. Diamonds rank among the country's leading exports, and the president personally intervenes in licensing and in the profits of the trade.

They want low export taxes, freedom to buy from artisanal miners, protection from expropriation and close relations with the regime, whose favour they purchase with gifts and shares. They favour Western markets and investors. Their leverage lies in foreign exchange, in the president's personal finances and in the smuggling routes they can open or close.

16.name: Les Commerçants haoussas
16.text:
Les Commerçants haoussas are the Hausa, Bornouan and Arab traders who dominate the cattle, kola and cloth trade of Bangui's markets and of the towns along the routes to Chad, Cameroon and Sudan. Organized through family firms and Muslim brotherhoods, they finance much of the country's internal commerce outside the French trading houses.

They want free trade, low taxes and licences, an end to price controls and extortion at roadblocks and equal treatment with European and Lebanese firms. Neutral in the Cold War, they deal pragmatically with whoever rules. Their leverage lies in their control of food supplies, livestock and informal credit in the capital and the provinces.

17.name: Les Amis de Saint-Floris
17.text:
Les Amis de Saint-Floris are the wildlife wardens, hunting guides and scientists concerned with the vast savanna reserves of the north, centred on the Saint-Floris national park, home to elephants, rhinoceroses, giraffes and great herds of antelope. Commercial hunting, ivory poaching from across the borders and concessions granted to friends of the regime are depleting the wildlife.

They call for real protection of the parks, controls on the ivory trade, limits on hunting concessions and support for rural communities living beside the reserves. They appeal to international conservation bodies rather than to either bloc. Their leverage is small, resting on foreign scientific interest and the prestige of the country's wildlife.

18.name: Mouvement d'Évolution Démocratique de l'Afrique Centrale
18.english: Democratic Evolution Movement of Central Africa
18.native_full: Mouvement d'Évolution Démocratique de l'Afrique Centrale
18.text:
The Democratic Evolution Movement of Central Africa was founded in 1960 by Abel Goumba, Boganda's former deputy and head of government, after his break with David Dacko. It briefly formed the only parliamentary opposition before it was dissolved and Goumba was jailed; released in 1962, he has lived abroad in medical and public-health work while former members keep quiet contacts in Bangui.

MEDAC stands for an independent, democratic socialism rooted in Boganda's ideals: honest government, cooperatives, land and education for peasants and a foreign policy free of French tutelage and bloc alignment. Its leverage lies in Goumba's reputation for integrity among intellectuals, students and teachers.

19.name: Les Amis de Pékin
19.text:
Les Amis de Pékin are the cadres, students and former officials who built close ties with the People's Republic of China under Dacko, when Bangui recognized Beijing in 1964 and Chinese specialists ran agricultural and aid projects. Bokassa broke relations and expelled the Chinese mission after the 1966 coup, accusing it of preparing a people's militia, and the group has since lived under suspicion.

They admire Maoist self-reliance, rural communes and people's war, and want a Central Africa independent of both France and the Soviet Union. Their leverage lies in the memory of Chinese aid, in their influence among radical teachers and students and in Beijing's readiness to return.

20.name: Les Fils de Boganda
20.text:
Les Fils de Boganda are the populist militants of MESAN's youth and women's organizations and of Bangui's market districts who venerate Barthélemy Boganda, the priest-politician killed in a plane crash in 1959, as a national saint. Their rallies mix Christian imagery, nationalist songs and denunciations of foreign merchants, corrupt functionaries and the colonial past.

They want a strong leader who speaks for the 'little people', jobs reserved for Central Africans, control of foreign traders and the realization of Boganda's dream of a great Central African state. They are suspicious of intellectuals and of both blocs. Their leverage lies in the crowds Bokassa mobilizes to legitimize his rule.

21.name: Les Ultras de l'Oubangui
21.text:
Les Ultras de l'Oubangui are the zealots of the military regime's personality cult: young officers, MESAN activists and broadcasters at Radio Bangui who demand total loyalty to the general-president and see conspiracies in every foreign community. They lead denunciation campaigns against Chadian, Congolese and Portuguese traders and against officials accused of sabotage.

They call for a militarized nation, public punishment of thieves and traitors, compulsory mobilization of youth and the expulsion of foreigners who 'exploit' the country. Anti-communist and contemptuous of democracy, they glorify discipline and the army. Their leverage lies in the president's tendency to adopt their most brutal proposals as policy.

22.name: Forces Armées Centrafricaines
22.text:
The Central African Armed Forces have ruled the country since the night of 31 December 1965, when their chief of staff, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, overthrew President David Dacko in the Saint-Sylvestre coup. Bokassa, a veteran of the Free French and of Indochina, now rules as president, general and holder of most key ministries, having executed his co-conspirator Alexandre Banza in 1969.

The regime promises order, development and the cleansing of corruption, leans on France for budget support and military aid, and courts any donor, East or West, who offers money. Its power rests on the officer corps, the gendarmerie and fear, though the army is small, poorly paid and divided by ethnic rivalries.

23.name: Maison Bokassa
23.text:
The House of Bokassa is the family and Mbaka clan of President Jean-Bédel Bokassa from Bobangui in the Lobaye, kin of Barthélemy Boganda and of the deposed David Dacko. Its members, including the president's many wives and children, hold lucrative posts, plantations and trading licences, and the president presents his family as the natural heir to Boganda's legacy.

Its partisans favour hereditary, personal rule modelled on Napoleon, whom Bokassa openly admires, with the head of state above parties, army and law. They cultivate France and any foreign patron who flatters the president. Their leverage lies in proximity to the palace and in Bokassa's absolute personal power.
